title: Brad Blickstein on Private Equity Thinking, AI Pricing, and the Law Firm Business Model
author: Brad Blickstein

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source does not substantively engage the cluster’s central framework of bounded AI assistance, human verification and responsibility, or the tension around junior development and leverage. Instead, it redirects attention to competitive service strategy: law firms and ALSPs should proactively create AI-enabled offerings, demonstrate advantages over insourcing, and respond to client demand. Its efficiency and quality claims are recommendations rather than empirical evidence of productivity gains.
qs: I’d build things, find new use cases, and bring solutions to clients before someone else does or before the client tries to build something themselves.
Explain why the firm can do it more efficiently, better, and at a better price than the law department going through the trouble of bringing it inside.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Blickstein anticipates AI-enabled firms operating without associates and pressure on law-firm leverage, aligning with the cluster’s premise that junior production may shrink. However, he does not address whether this threatens expertise reproduction or endorse deliberate simulation, mentorship and independent practice as the response.
qs: Can partners leave a BigLaw firm, start a firm with no associates and use AI instead, then go to the same clients who trust them with that new model?
If you’re a firm, that doesn’t work under the leverage model.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The excerpt contains only a host’s value-focused appraisal and Blickstein’s resource links. It does not articulate a position on whether legal AI benefits require organisational adaptation, human control, interdisciplinary preparation or changes to pricing and staffing models.
qs: Brad Blickstein, thank you so much for joining us again and helping us cut through the noise and think like value-focused operators.
Brad Blickstein (39:31)  Yeah, you can go to our website, BlicksteinGroup.com, or for the book itself, BlicksteinGroup.com/WWPED.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s service-redesign thesis and materially extends it with a provider-side response to client insourcing: law firms and ALSPs should proactively build AI-enabled offerings and demonstrate superior efficiency, quality and pricing before clients develop internal alternatives.
qs: I’d build things, find new use cases, and bring solutions to clients before someone else does or before the client tries to build something themselves.
Explain why the firm can do it more efficiently, better, and at a better price than the law department going through the trouble of bringing it inside.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Blickstein accepts that AI value requires providers to redesign offerings and client relationships, not merely acquire tools. He materially extends the cluster by prescribing proactive solution development to pre-empt client insourcing and by linking reduced billed hours to pressure on law-firm leverage, while qualifying the timing and mechanism as uncertain.
qs: I’d build things, find new use cases, and bring solutions to clients before someone else does or before the client tries to build something themselves.
Perhaps less so within the next two years, but eventually many law departments will put pressure on firms to reduce the number of hours they bill.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Blickstein accepts selective deployment and operating-model redesign, then materially extends the cluster by identifying fragmented law-firm authority, practice silos, AI-cost scrutiny, productivity measurement and hourly-billing incentives as concrete barriers to converting task-level capability into firmwide value.
qs: We understand why they’re put together in a firm, but in many ways they’re not alike enough for some of these systemic changes to be achieved entirely firmwide.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s shift from product announcements and flat licensing toward realized operational value and cost control. It identifies consumption-based pricing and everyday prompting practices as potential hidden cost drivers, while offering anecdotes and predictions rather than quantified economic evidence. Its private-equity framing is introductory and does not materially extend the cluster’s procurement proposition.
qs: Recently, Legora also announced that it’s moving its Agent Pro offering to consumption-based pricing, which means it’s billing by what the agent does rather than by a flat-seat license.

We’ve covered topics like what tokens are and why they function as a hidden meter running behind every chat, when to reset a conversation versus continue in the same chat, and what everyday prompting habits, from repasting whole documents to burying five questions in one prompt, might be driving up both cost and inaccuracy without you knowing it.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Blickstein supports the cluster’s central view that AI will pressure delivery economics, particularly through buyer-side insourcing, reduced billed hours and challenges to associate leverage. He also endorses proactive, solution-oriented offerings from firms and ALSPs, while treating market transformation and AI-native competition as qualified forecasts rather than established outcomes.
qs: I’d build things, find new use cases, and bring solutions to clients before someone else does or before the client tries to build something themselves.
Perhaps less so within the next two years, but eventually many law departments will put pressure on firms to reduce the number of hours they bill.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Blickstein supports the cluster’s core claim that AI-enabled reductions in billed associate work could pressure law firms’ leverage model. He also raises associate-light AI-native spin-offs as a possible competitive mechanism, but does not directly examine apprenticeship, partner succession or proposed training remedies; his claims remain qualified forecasts rather than established outcomes.
qs: Perhaps less so within the next two years, but eventually many law departments will put pressure on firms to reduce the number of hours they bill.
If you’re a firm, that doesn’t work under the leverage model.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source accepts that AI is changing competition among law firms, ALSPs and in-house teams, including a credible risk of client insourcing. It reinforces the cluster’s view that outcomes remain contested by arguing that providers can retain work through proactive solution design and a demonstrable efficiency, quality and pricing proposition. Its claims are strategic recommendations and observations, not evidence of completed market-wide change.
qs: I’d build things, find new use cases, and bring solutions to clients before someone else does or before the client tries to build something themselves.
Explain why the firm can do it more efficiently, better, and at a better price than the law department going through the trouble of bringing it inside.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Blickstein supports the synthesis that AI chiefly disrupts legal-service production economics rather than eliminating lawyers. He specifically links productivity gains to reduced hourly revenue and pressure on associate leverage, while advocating new pricing, measurement and proactive AI-enabled offerings by firms and ALSPs. His uncertainty about timing, buyer pressure and unresolved pricing mechanisms is consistent with the cluster’s qualified, incremental outlook.
qs: If you’re a firm, that doesn’t work under the leverage model.

kp.k: Core legal work offers opportunities for scalable delivery
kp.d: Blickstein uses Jae Um’s cream, core and commodity segmentation to distinguish bespoke high-end advice from systematized commodity work and potentially scalable middle-market work. He explicitly calls the suggested 70% core-market share a guess, not a measured finding. His bakery analogy supports identifying work suitable for technology and different resources rather than treating all work artisanally; he argues appropriate scaling could increase firm profitability.
qs: To be honest with you, that’s a Fermi number, or really just a guess.
This is what law departments spend most of their money on and, frankly, where law firms earn most of their profits. This is where the leverage model plays in for law firms.
That work can be more profitable for firms if it’s done right, and it needs to be differentiated from the artisanal cream work, which shouldn’t be scaled.

kp.k: Private-equity thinking need not require outside investment
kp.d: Responding to Lambert’s framing of annual partner distributions as an investment obstacle and his reported Kirkland $500 million AI infrastructure commitment, Blickstein suggests outside funding can support investment or smooth partner payouts. However, he emphasizes selective operational changes without outside capital and advance expectation-setting around distributions rather than a universal investment strategy.
qs: You can use PE funds, or funds from whomever, for some original payout to your partners, to smooth that over time, or to make the investment.
But one of the book’s big arguments is that you don’t need to take outside investment to do some of the things a PE fund would say a firm should be doing.
I list about 10 different things, but you don’t have to do them all at once.

kp.k: Professional pricing should replace unsupported partner intuition
kp.d: Blickstein recommends empowered professional pricing operations, not simply adoption of flat fees or AFAs. He asserts most firms and most midsized firms lack pricing groups, while existing groups may lack influence. He suggests potential improvements of a couple, three or five points through better pricing, but provides no supporting measurement or specified metric.
qs: In a lot of cases, those pricing groups have been neutered or aren’t listened to.
At most firms, it’s still often a partner’s gut feeling about whether they have to discount or whether they can pass through a price increase.
But for many firms, it’s easy to see a couple, three, or five points across the board if you bring in the right type of pricing function.

kp.k: Technology priorities face silos and managerial authority gaps
kp.d: Gebauer reports that the July 2026 Law Firm COO Survey first ranked technology investment and adoption above talent acquisition, with 38.1% identifying practice silos as the leading structural issue to fix and 27% citing insufficient operational authority. Blickstein attributes implementation difficulties to limited COO empowerment, greater support from leadership than individual partners, and materially different practice structures. The transcript supplies no survey sample size or methodology.
qs: For the first time, technology investment and adoption surpassed talent acquisition as the top strategic initiative for law firms.
Yet 38.1% of the COOs identified practice silos as the number-one structural issue they would fix, and 27% cited a lack of operational authority.
Leadership is often more supportive of COOs’ business initiatives than the partners are.
The IP practice and the M&A practice, for example, are run and built quite differently.

kp.k: Operational reform requires authority or exceptional consensus building
kp.d: Responding to Lambert’s report of more COOs entering from outside legal, Blickstein warns that corporate hierarchical experience may poorly fit partnership governance. His explicitly simplified comparison suggests plaintiffs’ firms more readily introduce business talent and innovation because power is concentrated and practices are less varied. He advises COOs to choose battles carefully in light of political capital and reputation.
qs: When the job becomes a consensus-building job, it’s difficult.
One instructive example, and I’m oversimplifying, is that plaintiffs’ firms don’t have this problem as often.
It takes a consolidation of power, or you need to be a world-class consensus builder, or there has to be some consolidation of power above you within the firm.

kp.k: AI productivity threatens hourly revenue without pricing changes
kp.d: Gebauer reports that 66% of surveyed COOs say their firms do not formally measure or document AI efficiency gains, while 39% expect greater lawyer productivity to increase revenue. Blickstein predicts measurement will improve, noting existing time records, but questions the revenue expectation under hourly billing. Additional clients might offset reduced hours, although he calls that unresolved; he expects firms may need AFAs to retain efficiency gains rather than merely satisfy clients.
qs: One of the most striking statistics in the COO Survey is that 66% of COOs report their firms do not formally measure or document AI-related efficiency gains.
And 39% of those same COOs expect AI to increase revenue through greater lawyer productivity.
Better productivity should decrease revenue. Perhaps it lets you bring on more clients and make enough of it back that way, but that’s a nuanced issue.
It might become the only way to make money.

kp.k: Longstanding AFA advocacy has not secured widespread client-driven change
kp.d: Blickstein recalls a 1992 Corporate Legal Times article titled “Alternative Billing Making a Comeback” to illustrate the longevity of AFA expectations. He argues that more than 30 years of experience has largely disproven the hypothesis that clients will force widespread adoption, while acknowledging adoption around the edges. His reference to “15% or whatever” is an informal estimate, not a documented survey result.
qs: in the fourth issue we published, in 1992, we ran an article with the headline, “Alternative Billing Making a Comeback.”
It’s true around the edges, and there’s 15% or whatever that do it, but the hypothesis that firms will adopt AFAs because clients will make them has been disproven over the last 30-plus years.

kp.k: Shadow billing exposes distrust in value-based arrangements
kp.d: Lambert identifies client demands for hours alongside alternative fees as a trust obstacle. Blickstein argues shadow billing effectively caps fees without providing a floor and recommends resisting such demands while explaining value transparently. He acknowledges he does not know how to resolve the broader problem; Gebauer challenges the practicality of resistance when pitches and RFPs explicitly require time information.
qs: If you’re a firm, you’re effectively putting a cap on the amount you can bill without putting a floor on the amount you could bill.
If you’re a firm and a client asks for shadow billing, the proper answer is no.
The whole point of an AFA is valuing the work rather than the time.
I’m preaching at this point, though. I don’t know how to do that.

kp.k: AI value extends beyond reducing lawyer hours
kp.d: Blickstein recommends discussing client cost savings, earlier completion and wider analytical coverage instead of hours saved. His illustrative due-diligence comparison contrasts reviewing the 25 largest client contracts with using AI to review all contracts; it is a proposed value proposition rather than a measured outcome. He recognizes that declining time-based RFP questions is commercially difficult and may lose some clients.
qs: Let’s not talk about how much time we’re saving. Let’s talk about how much money we’re saving.
Can you get the work done faster? I don’t mean in less time. I mean finished sooner.

Classic due diligence used to mean, “Send us the contracts with your 25 biggest clients,” because that was all the due diligence team had time to review. Now you can use AI to look at all the contracts.
What’s the value proposition around using AI that isn’t tied solely to efficiency?

kp.k: Corporate AI pilots depend on usable underlying data
kp.d: Gebauer reports that the 18th Annual Law Department Operations Survey places corporate GenAI piloting at 52% and fully operationalized systems at 23%. Blickstein rejects prematurely labeling this purgatory only two or three years into the AI era, predicts the pilot share will fall, and identifies tool-selection uncertainty and poor corporate data as obstacles. He also expects in-house productivity measurement to be harder than at firms because departments do not track daily work similarly. No survey sample size or methodology is provided.
qs: Meanwhile, corporate GenAI adoption is defined by piloting, at 52%, rather than fully operationalized systems, at 23%.
First, considering we’re only two or three years into the AI era, depending on how you count, I’m not sure it’s purgatory.
I wonder how many pilots will fail because the technology, adoption, and training are good, but the data isn’t there.
it’s going to be a much bigger problem in-house, where they don’t track what people do daily.

kp.k: AI-assisted data cleanup remains a hope, not finding
kp.d: Blickstein predicts greater comfort with data use and criticizes demanding maximum AI efficiency while withholding client data from training. Separately, he hopes AI can improve the data hygiene needed for legal applications, drawing an analogy to technology both creating and substantially addressing e-discovery’s data-volume problem. These are expectations and normative views, not demonstrated resolutions of security or data-quality concerns.
qs: The idea that we want our law firms to provide every possible ounce of efficiency through AI tools, but we won’t allow them to use our data as training data to help them do that, isn’t fair.
Technology then largely solved it with tools such as auto review and platforms.
I’m hoping AI will help solve the data hygiene problem itself, enabling AI to work better on the legal problems the data supports.

kp.k: Proactive offerings could counter clients bringing work in-house
kp.d: Lambert reports that usability first exceeded security as the top AI priority for surveyed legal operations teams. Blickstein asserts clients are receptive to proactive solutions and recommends firms and ALSPs develop offerings before buyers build internally or seek alternatives. Firms should justify retaining work through better quality, efficiency and price; this is strategic advice rather than quantified evidence of client demand.
qs: usability received a higher score and beat out security as the top AI priority for legal operations teams.
Explain why the firm can do it more efficiently, better, and at a better price than the law department going through the trouble of bringing it inside.
If I were a firm or an ALSP, I would build offerings and bring them to the right clients before the client decides to find a solution.

kp.k: ALSP growth coexists with client preference for firms
kp.d: Blickstein distinguishes apparently stagnant ALSP share of the overall legal market from strong growth at individual ALSP businesses. He attributes limits on displacement to clients’ preference for law firms and says ALSPs perform well in clearly process-oriented work, citing document review and e-discovery. Broader expansion requires convincing clients that substantial legal work benefits from process and technology rather than bespoke delivery. No market-share or growth figures are supplied.
qs: When you look at them as a percentage of the legal market’s overall share, it seems somewhat stagnant. But many of these businesses are on big growth curves within the ALSP segment.
For work that is clearly process-oriented, I think ALSPs are doing quite well.
They have to convince clients that a large amount of legal work isn’t artisanal, that it benefits from process and technology, and that ALSPs are the people to deliver it.

kp.k: Consumption pricing challenges assumptions about AI cost advantages
kp.d: Blickstein identifies growing cost scrutiny as a change from a year earlier and tentatively references Legora’s move toward consumption pricing. He argues token-based charges may alter deployment economics: AI could cease being cheaper than lawyers if costs rise sufficiently. Whether price increases persist or open models become more viable remains an open question, not a forecast with supporting cost comparisons.
qs: Legora, I believe, talked about moving to a consumption model.
The underlying assumption is that using AI to do this work is less expensive than using lawyers. At some point, if AI gets expensive enough, that might no longer be true.
Will these price increases stick? Will open models become more valuable and viable? Those are good questions.

kp.k: Tool adoption does not establish AI fluency
kp.d: Blickstein observes a shift from activation and usage metrics toward questions about proficiency, appropriate applications and sufficient use. His 98% usage example illustrates the inadequacy of adoption statistics rather than reporting a particular organization’s results. He expects attention to fluency and usefulness to influence assessments of tool value.
qs: we’re starting to see people distinguish between adoption and fluency.

“98% of our people have used the tool in the past month.” That’s a nice statistic, but it doesn’t say whether people have become AI-proficient or AI-fluent, whether they’re using it for the right things, or whether they’re using it enough.

kp.k: Faster legal software development is asserted, not measured
kp.d: Lambert recalls Blickstein’s prediction from the end of the previous year of about an 80% improvement in turnaround speed from idea to product. Blickstein regards the prediction as fulfilled, especially including internal firm and department development through vibe coding and Claude Code. The transcript provides no measured turnaround data substantiating the percentage.
qs: you thought there would be about an 80% improvement in turnaround speed from idea to product.

That does seem to be happening. Especially if you count the things being built within firms and law departments through vibe coding, Claude Code, or all those things, I think we can check that off as one I got right.

kp.k: Associate-free spin-offs could pressure traditional leverage models
kp.d: Blickstein predicts eventual client pressure to reduce billed hours will confront firms’ leverage economics, while qualifying that this may not occur within the next two years. He speculates that trusted BigLaw partners could establish firms using AI instead of associates and bring existing clients with them. Such competitive pressure might drive business-model change more strongly than client demands; the transcript does not establish this as observed displacement.
qs: Perhaps less so within the next two years, but eventually many law departments will put pressure on firms to reduce the number of hours they bill.
If you’re a firm, that doesn’t work under the leverage model.
Can partners leave a BigLaw firm, start a firm with no associates and use AI instead, then go to the same clients who trust them with that new model?
External forces like that might push firms to make some of these changes more than their clients do.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Blickstein predicts that AI efficiency will put pressure on hourly revenue and associate leverage, potentially making alternative pricing economically necessary for firms.
pts.d: Blickstein argues that greater productivity should reduce revenue under hourly billing unless firms offset the reduction with additional clients. He predicts eventual buyer pressure to reduce billed hours and suggests that firms may need AFAs to capture some efficiency gains rather than adopting them only to satisfy clients. These are conditional business-model arguments, not measured revenue effects. He also expects firms to improve productivity measurement.

pts.k: Blickstein identifies AI value beyond fewer hours: earlier completion and broader review coverage.
pts.d: He proposes that firms frame AI-enabled services around client cost savings, faster deal or litigation completion, and reviewing more contracts in due diligence. His statement that AI can review all contracts is an illustrative capability claim, not a reported evaluation of completeness or quality. He recommends building trust and explaining value independently of hours.

pts.k: Blickstein expects legal-department piloting to diminish, but warns that poor corporate data can prevent successful implementation.
pts.d: He does not accept that current piloting necessarily represents entrenched failure. He expects progress over time, anticipates resolution of data-protection concerns, and argues that data hygiene will become a growing constraint. He separately expresses hope, rather than a firm prediction, that AI itself can improve data hygiene.

pts.k: Consumption pricing may undermine the assumption that AI is cheaper than lawyer labour, while fluency becomes more important than adoption counts.
pts.d: Blickstein observes increasing cost concern among firms and in-house teams and cites Legora's contemplated consumption model with an explicit qualification. He conditionally suggests sufficiently expensive AI could lose its cost advantage over lawyers. He also sees a shift toward assessing whether people use AI proficiently and for suitable tasks, which he expects to affect perceived tool value. He does not predict a specific token price or cost crossover.

pts.k: AI-enabled offerings and associate-free spin-offs could alter competition for corporate legal work.
pts.d: Blickstein recommends that firms and ALSPs proactively offer better, cheaper services before clients build solutions or bring work in-house. He raises, as a speculative scenario rather than an established trend, partners leaving BigLaw to serve existing clients with AI instead of associates. Such entrants might exert more pressure on incumbent business models than clients do.

pts.k: Blickstein endorses the view that generative AI is accelerating legal software development, including internal development.
pts.d: Responding to a host's recap of his earlier prediction of approximately 80% faster idea-to-product turnaround, Blickstein says the change appears to be happening and points to work built inside firms and legal departments using vibe coding and Claude Code. His response endorses the direction of the prediction but supplies no measured turnaround results establishing that percentage.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists primarily of practitioner reasoning, historical experience, illustrative examples, and survey context rather than measured AI outcomes.
pts.d: The hosts introduce survey figures: 66% of COOs do not formally measure or document AI efficiency gains, 39% expect productivity-driven revenue increases, and corporate GenAI adoption is 52% piloting versus 23% fully operationalized. These are host-presented context, not independent quantitative claims attributed here to Blickstein. Blickstein grounds his measurement forecast in firms' existing time records and his pricing argument in decades following AFAs. His ten-hours-to-one-hour example is hypothetical. He supports the hope for AI-assisted data hygiene by analogy to e-discovery, and the software-development claim with observations of internal building. No survey methodology, AI performance benchmark, cost comparison, or measured revenue impact is supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most forecasts are open-ended and conditional; current observations are distinguished from eventual change and speculative possibilities.
pts.d: In this transcript labelled 2026, Blickstein describes cost concern and the adoption-to-fluency shift as current developments, contrasting cost concern with a year earlier. He provides no duration for that concern. He expects fewer pilots and better efficiency measurement over time without deadlines. Billing-model pressure is eventual and perhaps less likely within two years. Capturing AI value depends on pricing changes, client trust, and usable data; the loss of AI's labour-cost advantage depends on sufficiently high prices. He explicitly acknowledges uncertainty about how to achieve the proposed value-based client relationship.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central affected groups are corporate law firms, their associates and partners, corporate legal buyers, ALSPs, and legal-tool builders.
pts.d: Firms face pressure on hourly revenue, staffing leverage, pricing and measurement. Associates are implicated in the hypothetical AI-substituted spin-off, not in a quantified employment forecast. Partners could establish competing providers using existing client trust. Corporate legal departments face data-quality constraints and make build-versus-buy or insourcing decisions; Blickstein expects measuring their efficiency to be harder because they lack daily time records. Clients may benefit from lower costs, earlier completion and broader review. Firms and ALSPs can compete for scalable core work, though his estimate that core work constitutes roughly 70% of the market is explicitly a guess and concerns market segmentation, not staffing shape. He differentiates scalable core work from artisanal cream work rather than predicting universal automation.
